newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Red Cross seeks emergency funds for 9 mln people.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross seeks emergency funds for 9 mln people.

text.p: The global Red Cross organisation appealed on Tuesday for over $200 million to finance relief programmes around the world in 1997 to help some nine million "forgotten victims" of conflict and natural disasters.

Launching the appeal, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said a good response was vital to enable it to maintain a long-term effort in areas like Africa's Great Lakes, ex-Yugoslavia and ex-Soviet Central Asia.

Funds were always forthcoming from member societies and the international donor community for "appealing victims" in the midst of crises -- when civilians fled a war zone, after earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, the IFRC said.
But, its 288-page appeal added, "millions more around the globe are struggling to survive conditions of extreme and often life-threatening hardship.

"The emergency for them is counted not in weeks or months, but more often than not in years. And time makes these the less popular victims, especially once they are out of the media limelight," the Geneva-based Federation declared.

The IFRC, which links some 180 societies aroung the globe, focuses its work on disaster relief. The Swiss-run and also Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) works to protect civilians during wars and political strife.

Top priority under the new appeal, separate from the IFRC's campaign to raise $5.7 million for its emergency fund for disaster relief which allows for immediate release of cash in a crisis, is the central African refugee crisis, it said.

To cope with the cost of supporting some one million mainly Hutu refugees in and around Rwanda and Burundi, it was earmarking $41 million of the total appeal for reconstruction in the wake of the 1994 genocide and civil war.
The funds would also go towards distribution of food, seeds and farming instruments as well as to community health projects.

For former Yugoslavia, the IFRC said, it sought some $39 million for programmes in Bosnia, for re-integration of some 800,000 refugees and displaced people into their communities, for Serbia and Montenegro, and for Croatia.

Serbia and Montenegro, it said, were struggling to support 566,000 refugees -- mainly Serbs who fled areas of Croatia now back under Zagreb's control. But the IFRC had had to cut short help for these people "because of declining donor interest".

The third biggest programme was for Central Asia, for which the IFRC said it was seeking nearly $20 million to help some 1.2 million people hit by widespread poverty that has followed the collapse of the old communist system as well as ethnic strife.

For the Caucasus -- another former Soviet region which has produced the three independent states of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia -- the Federation said it needed some $10 million to help 435,000 people.

These were victims of natural, ethnic, political and economic disasters, some dating back to before the collapse of Soviet rule in 1991 and including thousands of people still living in makeshift homes since the 1988 Armenian earthquake.

The IFRC said the largest single group for which it was seeking funds were the some 1.5 to two million Afghans displaced or reduced to poverty by the two decades of civil war which shows little sign of ending.

For the Asia-Pacific region, it said, it was launching for the first time a separate "Monsoon appeal" for $3.5 million to serve as a standby fund to provide relief items for some 635,000 people within the first days of a disaster.

The Federation said it would push ahead with its appeal for some $9.2 million for support to 130,000 victims of the 1995 and 1996 floods in North Korea. Last week, it said only $700,000 had been raised as it described the situation as "critical."
